Fact Meaning / rule a | b ("a divides b") b = a·k for some integer k; in code b %
a | b and a | c then a | (b + c) and a | (b − c)
(a − b) % m = ((a % m) − (b % m) + m) % m divisors come in pairs d and n / d; one of them ≤ √n

Divisibility is the heart of number theory problems. The mod rules let you keep numbers small: take % m after every addition and multiplication and the final remainder is still right. Division does not work this way.
Divisors pair up as d and n/d, so trying d up to √n finds them all (第4章). For "how many numbers in a list divide x" over many x, turn it around and walk the multiples of each value instead.

Walking multiples v, 2v, 3v, … for every v up to M costs M/1 + M/2 + … ≈ M ln M, fast for M = 106 (P2926). Counting divisors of every number 1 … n by "how many multiples does i have" turns into Σ ⌊n / i⌋ (P1403).
Primality, the sieve of Eratosthenes, the linear sieve, segmented sieves.
cross out multiples of 2, 3, … ; green numbers are prime
A prime has exactly two divisors, 1 and itself; other numbers above 1 are composite. Testing one number takes O(√n). To find all primes up to N, sieve: for each prime p, cross out its multiples.
Whatever is never crossed out is prime.
Linear sieve (欧拉筛): cross out each composite exactly once, by its smallest prime factor; O(N). It also gives every number's smallest prime factor for free.

vector<bool> stores one bit per entry, so 108 flags fit in about 12 MB (P3383). A huge range [L, R] that is short (R − L ≤ 106) is sieved with only the primes up to √R, crossing out from the first multiple ≥ L: a segmented sieve (P1835). Remember that 1 is not prime.

title: 最大公约数与最小公倍数

text: Euclid, gcd × lcm = a × b, pairs with a given gcd and lcm.

The greatest common divisor gcd(a, b) is the largest number dividing both; the least common multiple lcm(a, b) is the smallest number both divide. Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), ending at gcd(a, 0) = a, in O(log). And gcd(a, b) × lcm(a, b) = a × b.

If gcd(P, Q) = x and lcm(P, Q) = y, then P = x·a and Q = x·b with a·b = y/x and gcd(a, b) = 1, so counting pairs means counting coprime splits of y/x (P1029). Write a / gcd(a, b) * b , dividing first, so the lcm does not overflow on the way (P4057). Reducing fractions (P1572) divides top and bottom by their gcd.
Unique prime factorisation; counting and summing divisors.
Fundamental theorem of arithmetic: every integer above 1 is a product of primes in exactly one way, n = p₁e₁ · p₂e₂ ⋯. Factor by trial division up to √n; whatever is left above 1 is one last prime.

From n = Π pᵢ^eᵢ Formula number of divisors Π (eᵢ + 1) sum of divisors Π (1 + pᵢ + … + pᵢ^eᵢ) gcd(a, b) each prime to the smaller exponent lcm(a, b) each prime to the larger exponent a divides b every exponent in a ≤ the one in b

A divisor of n picks each exponent from 0 to eᵢ independently, so the multiplication principle (第20章) gives Π(eᵢ + 1) divisors: 360 = 2³·3²·5 has 4·3·2 = 24. "How long until cells divide evenly into tubes" compares exponents of the same primes (P1069); the divisor sum of ab mod 9901 uses the sum formula with fast powers (P1593).
